title: 5.4–5.5 Catch-Up
contentObjective: I can show I am caught up on Lessons 5.4–5.5 by using each lesson's big idea in mixed practice.
languageObjective: I can explain which lesson's big idea I used and how, using key vocabulary from Lessons 5.4–5.5.

noticeAndWonder.context: Quick review from Lesson 5.5: This is an L-shaped room from a floor plan. A dashed line splits it into two rectangles, and each part is labeled with its length and width.
wonderStarters: I wonder what would happen if…

revealWordProblem.title: (Review from 5.5) Apply: Flooring
revealWordProblem.text: A designer is tiling an L-shaped lobby floor. The floor decomposes into a 12 ft by 8 ft rectangle and a 6 ft by 5 ft rectangle. If floor tiles cost $2.89 per square foot, what budget do you recommend the designer have for the tiles?
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: Decompose the L-shape: 12 × 8 = 96 sq ft and 6 × 5 = 30 sq ft. The pieces are joined, so add: 96 + 30 = 126 sq ft. Tiles cost $2.89 per sq ft, so 126 × $2.89 = $364.14. I recommend a budget of about $365 for the tiles.

turnAndTalk.question: The L-shaped room splits into a 12 ft by 8 ft rectangle and a 6 ft by 5 ft rectangle. Why is it easier to find the area after you decompose the L into two rectangles?
turnAndTalk.kernel: We decompose the L-shape because we already know how to find a rectangle's area.

stems.en: We decompose the L-shape into ___ because ___.
stems.es: Descomponemos la forma de L en ___ porque ___.

stems.en: After I split it, I can find each area using ___.
stems.es: Después de dividirla, puedo hallar cada área usando ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Students explain that the L-shape is hard to measure directly, so breaking it into two rectangles lets them use A = l x w on each piece and add the results.
turnAndTalk.extend: The wonder prompt asks if there is more than one way to split the L. Show a different decomposition and justify why both give the same total area.
extendStems: Another way to split it is ___, which gives ___ + ___.
Both ways give the same total because ___.

turnAndTalk.question: For the U-shaped pool you subtracted a 6 ft by 4 ft cutout from a 14 ft by 10 ft rectangle. How do you decide when to ADD areas and when to SUBTRACT?
turnAndTalk.kernel: We add when shapes are joined and subtract when a piece is removed.

stems.en: I subtracted the areas because a piece was ___, so 140 minus 24 equals ___.
stems.es: Resté las áreas porque una parte fue ___, entonces 140 menos 24 es ___.

stems.en: I add areas when ___, but I subtract when ___.
stems.es: Sumo áreas cuando ___, pero resto cuando ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: A strong answer states you subtract when a piece is cut out (pool = 140 - 24 = 116 sq ft) and add when shapes are joined, with a clear reason for each.
turnAndTalk.extend: Could you find the U-shaped pool's area by ADDING rectangles instead of subtracting a cutout? Justify whether both strategies reach the same answer.
extendStems: I could add by splitting the pool into ___, which gives ___.

turnAndTalk.question: The T-shaped conference room has a top of 14 ft by 4 ft and a stem of 6 ft by 10 ft, and carpet costs $5 per sq ft. Talk through finding the total cost.
turnAndTalk.kernel: Find each rectangle's area, add them, then multiply by the price.

stems.en: The top area is ___ square feet and the stem area is ___ square feet.
stems.es: El área de arriba es ___ pies cuadrados y el área del tronco es ___ pies cuadrados.

stems.en: I added the areas to get ___ square feet.
stems.es: Sumé las áreas para obtener ___ pies cuadrados.

stems.en: The cost is ___ times $5, which equals $___.
stems.es: El costo es ___ por $5, que es $___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Students compute top = 56 sq ft, stem = 60 sq ft, total = 116 sq ft, and cost = 116 x $5 = $580, explaining the add-then-multiply order.
turnAndTalk.extend: A house-shaped wall is a rectangle topped with a triangle. Explain how composite-figure thinking handles a figure made of two DIFFERENT shape types, not just rectangles.
extendStems: I would find the rectangle area with ___ and the triangle area with ___.

turnAndTalk.question: During practice on Area of Composite Figures, what strategy did you use when a problem felt tricky?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Break the figure into simple shapes. ADD the areas when shapes are joined; SUBTRACT when a piece is cut out.

stems.en: I knew my answer was reasonable because ___.
stems.es: Supe que mi respuesta era razonable porque ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Listen for students naming a specific strategy tied to 6.GR.1 — not just "I multiplied." They should connect steps to the key idea.
turnAndTalk.extend: How would you help a classmate who made the common mistake from today's lesson? Use one vocabulary word.
extendStems: I would tell them to ___ first because ___.
The mistake happens when you ___ instead of ___.

conceptIntro.heading: The Big Ideas — Lessons 5.4–5.5
conceptIntro.intro: Here is the one thing to remember from each lesson, plus a quick guided example. If one of these feels shaky, that lesson is right above this one in the menu — you can open it any time.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: 5.4: A regular polygon splits into the same number of triangles as it has sides, so total area = (one triangle's area) × (number of sides). • 5.5: Break the figure into simple shapes. ADD the areas when shapes are joined; SUBTRACT when a piece is cut out.

Stuck on one lesson's problems? Open that lesson from the curriculum menu for the full re-teach.

explore.instructions: Review from Lesson 5.5: Break each composite figure into simpler shapes. Find the area of each part, then calculate the total area.
explore.label: Decompose each composite figure and calculate the total area.

discourse.prompt: For the U-shaped pool, why did we subtract instead of add? When do you add areas and when do you subtract?
discourse.sentenceFrame: I ___ the areas because the composite figure is made by ___ a piece from a larger shape, so the total area is ___ - ___ = ___ square feet.

optional.stem: (Lesson 5.4) A regular hexagonal floor tile splits from its center into 6 congruent triangles, each with an area of 12 cm². What is the total area of the tile?
optional.explanation: A hexagon has 6 sides, so it splits into 6 equal triangles. Total = 6 × 12 = 72 cm².
choiceFeedback: Add them together for the total.

optional.stem: (Lesson 5.5) A 7 ft by 5 ft rectangle has a triangle (base 7 ft, height 4 ft) on top. Add the two areas. What is the total area?
optional.explanation: Rectangle = 7 x 5 = 35 sq ft. Triangle = 1/2 x 7 x 4 = 14 sq ft. The pieces are joined, so add: 35 + 14 = 49 sq ft.
choiceFeedback: Scale one dimension: area scales by that factor.
Scale both: area scales by the product.
Try: if both double, area goes × 4.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 5.4) A regular hexagon is divided into 6 equal triangles from the center. Each triangle has a base of 6 ft and a height of 5.2 ft. What is the area of one triangle?
approaching.explanation: A = ½ × b × h = ½ × 6 × 5.2 = 15.6 square feet.
choiceFeedback: Identify two rectangles and find each area.
hints: Focus on just ONE of the 6 triangles: its base is 6 ft and its height is 5.2 ft.
One triangle uses A = ½ × b × h — don't multiply by 6 yet; that step is for the whole hexagon.
Compute ½ × 6 × 5.2: take half of 6 first, then multiply by 5.2. Label it in sq ft.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 5.4) Using the triangle from the previous question, what is the total area of the hexagonal skylight?
approaching.explanation: Total area = 6 triangles × 15.6 sq ft = 93.6 square feet.
choiceFeedback: Is this a rectangle plus a triangle?
hints: You already found one triangle's area (15.6 sq ft) in the last question — now think about the whole hexagon.
A regular hexagon splits into 6 identical triangles, so the total is 6 copies of one triangle's area.
Multiply 15.6 × 6. (Tip: do 15 × 6, then 0.6 × 6, and combine.)

approaching.stem: (Lesson 5.5) An L-shaped room is made of two rectangles: 10 ft × 6 ft and 4 ft × 3 ft. What is the total area?
approaching.explanation: Area 1 = 10 × 6 = 60 sq ft. Area 2 = 4 × 3 = 12 sq ft. Total = 60 + 12 = 72 sq ft.
hints: The L-shape is already split into two rectangles for you: 10 × 6 and 4 × 3.
Find each rectangle's area separately with A = l × w, then combine — joined shapes mean adding.
Compute 10 × 6 and 4 × 3, then add the two results. Label your answer in sq ft.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 5.5) A rectangular patio is 15 ft × 10 ft with a 5 ft × 4 ft rectangular flower bed cut out. What is the remaining area?
approaching.explanation: Patio = 15 × 10 = 150 sq ft. Cutout = 5 × 4 = 20 sq ft. Remaining = 150 − 20 = 130 sq ft.
choiceFeedback: A thin rectangle and a square can differ.
hints: The flower bed is CUT OUT of the patio — that phrase tells you which operation to use.
Find the full patio area (15 × 10) and the cutout area (5 × 4), then remove the cutout.
Compute 15 × 10 and 5 × 4, then subtract the flower bed's area from the patio's area.

onLevel.hint: Identify shapes inside; use correct formula for each; add.
hints: Each row has two blanks: the area of ONE triangle first, then the total for the whole polygon.
Column 5 uses ½ × base × height. Column 6 multiplies that answer by the Number of Triangles.
Hexagon row: compute ½ × 6 × 5.2 for one triangle, then multiply your result by 6 for the total.
onLevel.title: (Lesson 5.4) Review problem

onLevel.label: (Lesson 5.4) Match each polygon to its total area.
onLevel.hint: Compute total area by breaking figure into simple shapes.
hints: Each polygon card shows its triangle count and one triangle's ½ × b × h setup — the match is the TOTAL area.
Work in two steps: evaluate the ½ × b × h part, then multiply by the number of triangles named.
Hexagon card: find ½ × 6 × 5.2 for one triangle, then multiply by 6 to get the total to match.

onLevel.hint: After scaling, calculate new area and compare to original.
hints: The Operation column already tells you whether to add or subtract — no deciding needed, just computing.
Add rows: Shape 1 + Shape 2. Subtract rows: Shape 1 − Shape 2 (the big shape comes first).
L-shaped deck row: add 48 + 20. Wall row: subtract 18 from 120.
onLevel.title: (Lesson 5.5) Review problem

onLevel.label: (Lesson 5.5) Match each composite figure to its total area.
onLevel.hint: Compute A = l x w for each rectangle; compare results.
hints: Each card names its rectangles, and the word 'minus' marks the cutout figures.
Multiply each pair of dimensions first, then add for joined shapes or subtract for cutouts.
First card: 10 × 6 = 60 and 4 × 3 = 12 — combine them, then match. Handle the 'minus' cards with subtraction.

extending.title: (Lesson 5.4) Find the Area Error
extending.correctWork: To find total area, multiply (not add): Total = 10.75 × 6 = 64.5 sq m. Six equal triangles means 6 times one triangle's area.
hints: Look at Step 4. What operation should you use to combine 6 equal triangles?
The student added 10.75 + 6 instead of multiplying 10.75 × 6.

extending.title: (Lesson 5.5) Find the Area Error

workedExample.label: Identify the shapes
workedExample.work: Rectangle: 16 ft × 10 ft, with a 4 ft × 6 ft piece cut from the corner

extending.correctWork: Since the piece is cut out, subtract: 160 − 24 = 136 sq ft. When a piece is removed, subtract its area from the larger shape.
hints: Look at Step 4. Was the smaller rectangle added on or cut away?
The problem says the piece was 'cut from the corner,' so you should subtract, not add.

optionalActivity.name: Catch-Up Challenge
optionalActivity.intro: Mix it up: pick the right lesson's big idea for each problem — that's the real catch-up skill.

practice.commonMistake: A common mistake in Area of Composite Figures is adding every piece even when a piece has been cut out of the figure. For a 10 ft by 8 ft rectangle with a 3 ft by 2 ft rectangular notch cut from one corner, students compute the full rectangle 10 × 8 = 80 sq ft and stop, or they add the notch instead of removing it (80 + 6 = 86 sq ft) instead of subtracting it: 80 − (3 × 2) = 80 − 6 = 74 sq ft. Before submitting, check whether each piece is part of the figure (add it) or missing from the figure (subtract it).

exitTicket.stem: (Catch-up check, from Lesson 5.4) A regular pentagon is decomposed into 5 triangles from its center. Each triangle has a base of 7 inches and a height of 4.8 inches. What is the total area of the pentagon?
exitTicket.explanation: One triangle: A = 1/2 x 7 x 4.8 = 16.8 sq in. Total = 5 x 16.8 = 84 square inches.
choiceFeedback: That's one triangle — multiply by all 5 triangles.
You skipped the ½ — each triangle is ½ × 7 × 4.8.
Right value, wrong unit — area is square inches.
hints: Two steps hide in this problem: one triangle's area first, then all 5 triangles together.
One triangle is ½ × 7 × 4.8; the pentagon is 5 of those. Skipping either step leads to a wrong path.
Take half of 7 × 4.8 to get one triangle's area, then multiply that by the 5 triangles.
